§2 · Resolve the target column's own declared affinity
This first question only matters for STRICT tables using a
custom/domain type (registered via CREATE TYPE) or an array
Turso needs the type's real base affinity
substring rules, because those rules can be fooled by a custom
type's name — a domain named "doubled" contains "DOUB", which
the rules below would wrongly read as REAL. The override
sidesteps that by carrying the correct affinity directly.
Not a STRICT table, or a plain built-in type like
INTEGER / TEXT / REAL? Then the answer is always No.
Start from the target column's declared type string
Does the column have a Turso custom-type
checked top to bottom, first match wins.
Substring match, not a keyword match —
or is the declared type string empty
§2.2 · Is the table STRICT and the
STRICT tables (CREATE TABLE ... STRICT) require every column to
have one of a fixed list of real types. ANY is the one escape
hatch: a STRICT column declared ANY can hold a value of any
Since it can hold anything, Turso does not try to parse or
convert it at all — it is always treated as BLOB, meaning
x always behaves as BLOB here, no matter what is put in it.
Is the target affinity Integer or Numeric?
Text gets trimmed and hex ("0x...") is excluded, then parsed
ONLY if the ENTIRE remaining string is a well-formed number
An integer is unconditionally converted to float. Text follows
the same trim/parse rule, but a successful parse always becomes
a float — it never stays an int, unlike the Integer/Numeric case
STRICT tables skip this entire box and run Insn::TypeCheck
instead — reject a type mismatch outright rather than coerce it.
The new value is physically written with this coercion applied
has_affinity is really asking: does this expression have a REAL,
A table column does. A literal like 5 or 'abc', a computed
expression like a + 1, or a function call result does not —
Turso cannot know its type just by looking at it, so for
comparison purposes it is treated as untyped
(has_affinity = false, affinity = BLOB), no matter what value it
Transparent — recurse into e and inherit its answer verbatim.
COLLATE's own name plays no role in this decision (§4.6)
Is it a Parenthesized([e]) with a single element,
What kind of expression is it?
Is this column backed by a real BTree table?
"Backed by a real BTree table" is asking: is this an actual
column of an actual on-disk table (CREATE TABLE), rather than
a column that only exists because of how the query is written?
In SELECT ... FROM t1, t1.a is backed by a real BTree — Yes.
In SELECT ... FROM (SELECT 1 AS x) d, d.x is not: it only
exists inside this query, so it is a FromClauseSubquery
column (same for a CTE or a VIEW) — No.
has_affinity = true — read the column's own declared
affinity with the same box the WRITE path uses, just
being read here instead of applied to a new value

§10.2 · Start at arm 1's affinity via the same lossy

BLOB-declared leading arm is indistinguishable from

An internal detail, not something you write in SQL. When
translating something like UPDATE t SET a = a + 1, Turso
sometimes needs to compare against the column's in-progress new
value before it is written back to the table, and that value
lives in a VDBE register rather than being read fresh from the
column. You only hit this branch reading generated bytecode.
Is this register mapping found in the resolver?
Found in the resolver, and exactly 1 result register
Inherit the inner query's result column's answer
VERBATIM, has_affinity bit included — this is the one place
a subquery's real type survives intact

§2 · Resolve the indexed column's own declared affinity
This first question only matters for STRICT tables using a
custom/domain type (registered via CREATE TYPE) or an array
Turso needs the type's real base affinity
substring rules, because those rules can be fooled by a custom
type's name — a domain named "doubled" contains "DOUB", which
the rules below would wrongly read as REAL. The override
sidesteps that by carrying the correct affinity directly.
Not a STRICT table, or a plain built-in type like
INTEGER / TEXT / REAL? Then the answer is always No.
Start from the indexed column's declared type string
Does the column have a Turso custom-type
checked top to bottom, first match wins.
Substring match, not a keyword match —
or is the declared type string empty
§2.2 · Is the table STRICT and the
STRICT tables (CREATE TABLE ... STRICT) require every column to
have one of a fixed list of real types. ANY is the one escape
hatch: a STRICT column declared ANY can hold a value of any
Since it can hold anything, Turso does not try to parse or
convert it at all — it is always treated as BLOB, meaning
x always behaves as BLOB here, no matter what is put in it.
Is the indexed column's own affinity Text?
This index is excluded from cost-based selection entirely for
this predicate, before cost-based selection even runs. Exactly
the same check, reading the exact same cached Constraint value,
whether the index came from a real CREATE INDEX or an
optimizer-synthesized auto-index for an unindexed join side (§9.3)
Only ok if the indexed column's own affinity is ALSO numeric —
otherwise the column's stored values were coerced to text at
insert time and a numeric seek key could never match them
§2 · Resolve the indexed column's own declared affinity
This first question only matters for STRICT tables using a
custom/domain type (registered via CREATE TYPE) or an array
Turso needs the type's real base affinity
substring rules, because those rules can be fooled by a custom
type's name — a domain named "doubled" contains "DOUB", which
the rules below would wrongly read as REAL. The override
sidesteps that by carrying the correct affinity directly.
Not a STRICT table, or a plain built-in type like
INTEGER / TEXT / REAL? Then the answer is always No.
Start from the indexed column's declared type string
Does the column have a Turso custom-type
checked top to bottom, first match wins.
Substring match, not a keyword match —
or is the declared type string empty
§2.2 · Is the table STRICT and the
STRICT tables (CREATE TABLE ... STRICT) require every column to
have one of a fixed list of real types. ANY is the one escape
hatch: a STRICT column declared ANY can hold a value of any
Since it can hold anything, Turso does not try to parse or
convert it at all — it is always treated as BLOB, meaning
x always behaves as BLOB here, no matter what is put in it.
Is the indexed column's own affinity numeric
The column's stored values were coerced to text at insert time,
so a numeric seek key could never match them by memcmp. The
index is excluded from cost-based selection entirely for this
predicate, before cost-based selection even runs — same check
for a real CREATE INDEX and for an optimizer-synthesized
auto-index on an unindexed join side (§9.3)
A range predicate's lower and upper bound are each their own
independent walk through this entire tree. There is no combined
Insn::Affinity is emitted on the seek-key register(s), coercing the
key toward the resolved comparison affinity using the same
apply_affinity_char rules from the top of this tree (skipped if
provably a no-op) — THEN the SeekGE / SeekGT / SeekLE / SeekLT
